claim: The original Brainbow method provided inadequate fluorescence levels for neuronal tracing.
source: The stochastic multicolor labeling method 'Brainbow' is a powerful strategy to label multiple neurons differentially with fluorescent proteins; however, the fluorescence levels provided by the original attempts to use this strategy were inadequate.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a limitation of existing methods that motivated the development of Tetbow.

claim: Tetbow is a stochastic multicolor labeling method with enhanced expression levels that uses a tetracycline-operator system.
source: In the present study, we developed a stochastic multicolor labeling method with enhanced expression levels that uses a tetracycline-operator system (Tetbow).
evidence: This is the primary methodological contribution described in the abstract.

claim: Tetbow was optimized for both plasmid and virus vector-mediated multicolor labeling.
source: We optimized Tetbow for either plasmid or virus vector-mediated multicolor labeling.
evidence: The abstract states this as a key feature of the method development.

claim: When combined with tissue clearing, Tetbow can visualize the three-dimensional architecture of individual neurons.
source: When combined with tissue clearing, Tetbow was powerful enough to visualize the three-dimensional architecture of individual neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a capability demonstrated in the study.

claim: Tetbow enabled visualization of axonal projection patterns of individual mitral/tufted cells along several millimeters in the mouse olfactory system.
source: Using Tetbow, we were able to visualize the axonal projection patterns of individual mitral/tufted cells along several millimeters in the mouse olfactory system.
evidence: This is presented as a specific application demonstrating the method's utility.

claim: A Tetbow system with chemical tags was developed in which genetically encoded chemical tags were labeled with synthetic fluorophores.
source: We also developed a Tetbow system with chemical tags, in which genetically encoded chemical tags were labeled with synthetic fluorophores.
evidence: This is described as an extension of the Tetbow method.

claim: The Tetbow system with chemical tags expands the repertoire of fluorescence labels and applications.
source: This was useful in expanding the repertoire of the fluorescence labels and the applications of the Tetbow system.
evidence: This is stated as a benefit of the chemical tag approach.

claim: These new tools facilitate light-microscopy-based neuronal tracing at both large scale and high resolution.
source: Together, these new tools facilitate light-microscopy-based neuronal tracing at both a large scale and a high resolution.
evidence: This is the concluding statement of the abstract summarizing the impact of the methods.

claim: Fluorescent proteins are useful for labeling genetically-defined neuronal populations.
source: In particular, fluorescent proteins are useful for labeling genetically-defined neuronal populations.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: A number of tissue-clearing methods have been developed in recent years and optimized for use with fluorescent proteins and deep-tissue antibody staining.
source: In recent years, a number of tissue-clearing methods have been developed, and these have been optimized for use with fluorescent proteins and deep-tissue antibody staining (Hama et al., 2011; Chung et al., 2013; Ke et al., 2013; Susaki et al., 2014; Richardson and Lichtman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: New tissue-clearing tools have expanded the scale of fluorescence imaging technologies to whole-organ and whole-organism levels.
source: These new tools have expanded the scale of the available technologies for fluorescence imaging to whole-organ and whole-organism levels.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of tissue-clearing method development.

claim: It is difficult to dissect and trace an individual neuron from a brain sample labeled with a single type of fluorescent protein.
source: It is still difficult, however, to dissect and trace an individual neuron from a brain sample labeled with a single type of fluorescent protein.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation motivating the need for multicolor labeling.

claim: SeeDB2 is a tissue-clearing agent developed for high-resolution three-dimensional fluorescence imaging.
source: Recently, we developed a tissue-clearing agent for high-resolution three-dimensional fluorescence imaging, named SeeDB2 (Ke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as prior work by the authors with citation.

claim: SeeDB2 was designed to minimize spherical aberrations, allowing for high-resolution imaging including super-resolution microscopy.
source: SeeDB2 was designed to minimize spherical aberrations, allowing for high-resolution imaging including super-resolution microscopy.
evidence: This describes the design principle and capability of SeeDB2.

claim: SeeDB2 improved z-resolution, which is critical for dissection of neuronal fibers crossing over along the z-axis.
source: In this approach, there was much improvement in the z-resolution, a critical factor for dissection of neuronal fibers crossing over along the z-axis.
evidence: This is stated as a specific benefit of the SeeDB2 approach.

claim: Expansion microscopy is a promising approach to improve resolution in three-dimensional fluorescence imaging.
source: Similarly, expansion microscopy is also a promising new approach used to improve resolution in three-dimensional fluorescence imaging (Chen et al., 2015; Ku et al., 2016; Tillberg et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior work.

claim: Brainbow is a transgenic multicolor labeling method in which three different fluorescent proteins are expressed in a stochastic manner.
source: To facilitate the dissection of individual neurons, a transgenic multicolor labeling method, Brainbow, has been developed, in which three different fluorescent proteins were expressed in a stochastic manner (Livet et al., 2007; Cai et al., 2013; Loulier et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the Brainbow method with citations.

claim: Brainbow uses the Cre-loxP system to express one of three fluorescent protein genes stochastically in a transgene.
source: Brainbow used the Cre-loxP system to express one of the three fluorescent protein genes stochastically in a transgene.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of Brainbow.

claim: When multiple copies of the Brainbow transgene cassette are introduced, stochastic choices result in combinatorial expression producing dozens of color hues.
source: When multiple copies of the transgene cassette are introduced, stochastic choices will result in a combinatorial expression of these three genes with different copy numbers, producing dozens of color hues.
evidence: This explains how color variation is achieved in Brainbow.

claim: Existing Brainbow methods are of limited use for neuronal tracing because expression levels of fluorescent proteins are not sufficiently high for bright and high-resolution imaging of axons and dendrites.
source: Although the Brainbow concept is powerful for discriminating between numerous neurons using light microscopy, the existing Brainbow methods are of limited use for neuronal tracing. This is because the stochastic and combinatorial expression of fluorescent proteins is possible only at low copy number ranges for the transgenes, so that the expression levels of the fluorescent proteins were not sufficiently high for bright and high-resolution imaging of axons and dendrites.
evidence: This is stated as a key limitation of existing Brainbow methods.

claim: Many previous Brainbow studies were forced to use subsequent antibody staining to produce reliable neuronal tracing.
source: Therefore, many of the previous studies were forced to use subsequent antibody staining to produce reliable neuronal tracing.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the low expression levels in Brainbow.

claim: Vector-mediated gene transfer has become a versatile tool in modern neuroscience.
source: As vector (plasmid and virus)-mediated gene transfer has become a versatile tool in modern neuroscience, we aimed to perform multicolor labeling using these tools.
evidence: This is stated as motivation for the approach taken.

claim: The authors demonstrated the ability to trace axons of individual neurons on the scale of several millimeters in the mouse olfactory system as a proof-of-concept experiment.
source: As a proof-of-concept experiment, we demonstrated the ability to trace axons of individual neurons on the scale of several millimeters in the mouse olfactory system.
evidence: This is stated as a specific demonstration of the method.

claim: The combination of Tetbow and tissue clearing facilitates neuronal tracing at higher densities and resolutions.
source: When combined with the advances in the growing field of tissue-clearing techniques, these new multicolor labeling strategies should facilitate neuronal tracing at higher densities and resolutions.
evidence: This is stated as the expected impact of the methods.

claim: Earlier Brainbow methods utilized transgenic animals for stochastic multicolor labeling.
source: Earlier Brainbow methods utilized transgenic animals for stochastic multicolor labeling.
evidence: This describes the approach of earlier Brainbow methods.

claim: In the Cre-loxP system, DNA recombination results in stochastic selection of one fluorescent protein gene out of three or more choices.
source: They utilized the Cre-loxP system, in which DNA recombination resulted in a stochastic selection of one fluorescent protein gene out of three (or more) choices.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the Cre-loxP system in Brainbow.

claim: Plasmid or virus vector-mediated gene transfer has become a more versatile strategy in neuroscience in recent years.
source: In recent years, however, plasmid or virus vector-mediated gene transfer has become a more versatile strategy in neuroscience.
evidence: This is stated as a trend in the field.

claim: An AAV-mediated Brainbow method (AAV-Brainbow) has been previously reported.
source: Previously, an adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated Brainbow method (AAV-Brainbow) has been reported (Cai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: In vector-mediated gene transfer, the Cre-loxP system is not essential for stochastic and combinatorial expression of XFP genes.
source: However, in the vector-mediated gene transfer, the Cre-loxP system is not essential for the stochastic and combinatorial expression of XFP genes (Kobiler et al., 2010; Weber et al., 2011; Siddiqi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Color variations can be made by introducing a mixture of three different XFP constructs as long as the copy number of introduced genes is small.
source: We can easily make color variations by introducing a mixture of three different XFP constructs: as long as the copy number of the introduced genes is small, labeled neurons will still produce a variety of colors irrespective of whether the Cre-loxP system is used or not (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated as a principle and supported by Figure 1A-C.

claim: Color variation reduces as the copy number of introduced genes increases.
source: It should be noted, however, that color variation reduces as the copy number of the introduced genes increases.
evidence: This is stated as an important consideration for the method.

claim: The number of introduced genes follows a Poisson distribution.
source: We considered that the number of introduced genes will follow a Poisson distribution (Kobiler et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an assumption with a citation.

claim: When three different XFP genes are introduced at 20 copies/cell/color on average, only a small degree of color variation will be generated.
source: When three different XFP genes are introduced at 20 copies/cell/color on average, a similar number of copies will be introduced into each neuron, and only a small degree of color variation will be generated (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated and supported by Figure 1C simulation.

claim: If the copy number is too small, many neurons will express just one XFP gene.
source: By contrast, if the copy number is too small, many of the neurons will express just one XFP gene (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated and supported by Figure 1A simulation.

claim: When three genes are introduced at an average 2 copies/cell/color, much larger color variations will be produced.
source: When these three genes are introduced at an average 2 copies/cell/color, much larger color variations will be produced (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated and supported by Figure 1B simulation.

claim: The mean Euclidean distance for two randomly chosen cells is greater when the copy number is lower.
source: The mean Euclidean distance (d) for two randomly chosen cells was greater when the copy number was lower (Figure 1D,E)
evidence: This is stated and supported by Figure 1D,E.

claim: When XFP genes are expressed at 2 copies/color/cell with a threshold distance of 0.1, 95.3% of cells can be discriminated from a given cell.
source: In our simulation, when we assumed a threshold distance of 0.1, 95.3% of cells could be discriminated from a given cell when XFP genes were expressed at 2 copies/color/cell (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the simulation shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Experienced researchers can discriminate two colors separated by 0.1 Euclidean distances in the color-coding space at 94.5 ± 1.73% accuracy.
source: We also found that experienced researchers can discriminate two colors separated by 0.1 Euclidean distances in the color-coding space at 94.5 ± 1.73% accuracy (mean ± S.D.; Figure 1H and Figure 1— figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Approximately 2 copies/color/cell is the optimum when color hues are judged visually by human experimenters.
source: Thus, ~2 copies/color/cell is the optimum when the color hues are judged visually by human experimenters.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the simulation and human discrimination data.

claim: In utero electroporation of plasmid vectors was used to introduce genes into layer 2/3 cortical pyramidal neurons at embryonic day 15.
source: We evaluated this prediction using the in utero electroporation of plasmid vectors into layer 2/3 cortical pyramidal neurons (electroporated at embryonic day 15).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: A mixture of three separate plasmid vectors encoding mTurquoise2, EYFP, and tdTomato genes under a CAG promoter was introduced.
source: We introduced a mixture of three separate plasmid vectors encoding mTurquoise2 (blue), EYFP (green), and tdTomato (red) genes under a CAG promoter.
evidence: This describes the specific constructs used in the experiment.

claim: When CAG plasmids were expressed at high copy numbers (1 μg/μL/plasmid), only small color variations were produced.
source: When these plasmids were expressed at high copy numbers (CAG High; DNA solution introduced was 1 μg/μL/plasmid; 3 μg/μL in total; see 'Materials and methods' section for details), only small color variations were produced (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: When CAG plasmid DNA concentrations were reduced to 0.25 μg/μL/plasmid, color variation increased but overall fluorescence levels were much reduced.
source: When the DNA concentrations were reduced (CAG Low; 0.25 μg/μL/plasmid), the color variation increased (Figure 2B), but the overall fluorescence levels were much reduced (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figures 2B and 2E.

claim: There is a trade-off between the expression levels of fluorescent proteins and color variations.
source: Thus, there is a trade-off between the expression levels of fluorescent proteins and color variations, and this is the reason why the previous Brainbow methods were unable to produce color variations that were bright enough for labeling.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The TRE promoter ensures much higher expression levels than the CAG promoter when expressed with tTA.
source: Recent studies indicated that the tetracycline response element (TRE) promoter ensures much higher expression levels than the CAG promoter when expressed with a tetracycline trans-activator (tTA) (Madisen et al., 2015; Sadakane et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: A WPRE sequence was introduced in the 3' UTR of XFP genes to improve their expression levels.
source: We also introduced a Woodchuck hepatitis virus posttranscriptional regulatory element (WPRE) sequence in the 3'′ UTR of XFP genes to improve their expression levels.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the Tetbow constructs.

claim: Earlier Brainbow techniques used membrane-bound XFPs because unmodified XFPs labeled the somata too brightly and affected the tracing of nearby neurites.
source: Earlier Brainbow techniques used membrane-bound XFPs because unmodified XFPs labeled the somata too brightly and affected the tracing of nearby neurites (Cai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation explaining the rationale for membrane-bound XFPs in Brainbow.

claim: The problem of bright somata can be solved by minimizing spherical aberration in microscopy using an index-matched clearing agent, SeeDB2.
source: However, this problem can be easily solved by minimizing spherical aberration in microscopy by using an index-matched clearing agent, SeeDB2 (Ke et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Unmodified XFPs label axons and dendrites much more brightly than membrane-bound XFPs.
source: Furthermore, unmodified XFPs label axons and dendrites much more brightly than the membrane-bound ones (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation, though data are not shown.

claim: Tetbow constructs achieved much higher XFP expression levels compared with CAG-promoter plasmids.
source: These new set of constructs (named Tetbow; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) achieved much higher XFP expression levels when compared with the CAG-promoter plasmids (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Tetbow showed a six-fold increase in EYFP fluorescence levels compared to CAG 0.25 μg/μL.
source: When we quantified the expression levels of EYFP, we observed a six-fold increase in fluorescence levels (Figure 2E; CAG 0.25 μg/μL vs. Tetbow 0.25 μg/μL; n = 104 and 260, respectively, p<0.0001, Kruskal Wallis with Dunn's post hoc test).
evidence: This is stated with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Tetbow allowed for much more robust multicolor labeling than Brainbow constructs when introduced by in utero electroporation.
source: Tetbow allowed for much more robust multicolor labeling than the Brainbow constructs when introduced by in utero electroporation, allowing more reliable axon tracing (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Tetbow system achieved bright labeling while maintaining color variations produced by low copy numbers of XFP genes.
source: Owing to the enhanced expression, the Tetbow system achieved bright labeling (Figure 2E) while maintaining the color variations produced by low copy numbers of XFP genes.
evidence: This is stated as a key advantage of Tetbow.

claim: When CAG-XFP genes were introduced at high concentrations (1 μg/μL each), color variations were small, whereas Tetbow constructs (0.25 μg/μL) produced much larger variations.
source: When CAG-XFP genes were introduced at high concentrations (1 μg/μL each), the color variations were small; by contrast, the Tetbow constructs (0.25 μg/μL) produced much larger variations (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Different cells are better discriminated by Tetbow than in the CAG High condition.
source: In the color discrimination analysis, we confirmed that different cells are better discriminated by Tetbow than in the CAG High condition (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Among four plasmid concentrations tested (0.05, 0.1, 0.25, and 0.5 μg/μL each), color discrimination performance was comparable.
source: Among the four plasmid concentrations we tested (0.05, 0.1, 0.25, and 0.5 μg/μL each), color discrimination performance was comparable.
evidence: This is stated as a result of testing different concentrations.

claim: Expression levels of XFP were highest at 0.25 μg/μL each, not at 0.5 μg/μL.
source: Paradoxically, however, the expression levels of XFP were the highest at 0.25 μg/μL each, not at 0.5.
evidence: This is stated as an unexpected finding.

claim: A moderate expression level of tTA is critical for optimum expression.
source: We therefore considered the possibility that a moderate expression level of tTA is critical for the optimum expression.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: When 0.1, 0.25, and 0.5 μg/μL of CAG-tTA plasmid was co-introduced with 0.25 μg/μL each of TRE-XFP plasmids, the highest expression level was found with 0.1 μg/μL CAG-tTA.
source: When 0.1, 0.25, and 0.5 μg/μL of CAG-tTA plasmid was co-introduced with 0.25 μg/μL each of TRE-XFP plasmids, the highest expression level was found with 0.1 μg/μL CAG-tTA (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Too high a concentration of tTA leads to suppression of TRE-XFP genes.
source: Thus, too high a concentration of tTA leads to the suppression of TRE-XFP genes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data.

claim: When the WPRE sequence was added to the CAG-tTA plasmid, the expression level of TRE-XFP genes was reduced.
source: Consistent with this assumption, when the WPRE sequence was added to the CAG-tTA plasmid, the expression level of TRE-XFP genes was reduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression level of tTA needs to be moderate to achieve the highest expression of TRE-XFP genes.
source: Thus, the expression level of tTA needs to be moderate to achieve the highest expression of TRE-XFP genes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: SeeDB2 is designed to minimize spherical aberrations for glycerol (SeeDB2G) or oil (SeeDB2S) immersion objective lenses.
source: SeeDB2 is designed to minimize spherical aberrations for glycerol (SeeDB2G) or oil (SeeDB2S) immersion objective lenses, making high-resolution 3D imaging possible.
evidence: This describes the design of SeeDB2.

claim: Various fluorescent proteins are best preserved in SeeDB2, much more so than in commercialized mounting media or other tissue-clearing agents.
source: Furthermore, various fluorescent proteins were best preserved in SeeDB2, much more so than in commercialized mounting media or other tissue-clearing agents (Ke et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: The combination of Tetbow and SeeDB2 is ideal for high-resolution volumetric multicolor imaging.
source: Therefore, the combination of Tetbow and SeeDB2 is ideal for high-resolution volumetric multicolor imaging.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the properties of both methods.

claim: After clearing with SeeDB2G, fluorescence levels of XFPs with Tetbow were strong enough to visualize fine detail of neuronal morphology in 3D.
source: After clearing with SeeDB2G, the fluorescence levels of XFPs with Tetbow were strong enough to allow visualization of the fine detail of neuronal morphology in 3D (Figure 4A and Video 1).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4A and Video 1.

claim: Detailed structures of dendritic spines were clearly visualized with Tetbow in adult brain slices (P70).
source: When we analyzed adult brain slices (P70), detailed structures of dendritic spines (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Video 2) and axonal boutons (Figure 4C) were clearly visualized with Tetbow.
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Video 2.

claim: High-resolution images of synaptic structures were obtained using solely native fluorescence of XFPs, with no antibody staining.
source: It should be noted that we obtained these high-resolution images of synaptic structures using solely native fluorescence of XFPs, with no antibody staining.
evidence: This is stated as an important feature of the method.

claim: Each glomerulus in the olfactory bulb is innervated by 20-50 M/T cells.
source: It is known that each glomerulus in the olfactory bulb is innervated by 20–50 M/T cells (Ke et al., 2013; Imai, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Dendrites from different mitral cells were clearly visualized and distinguishable by their different colors when looking at each glomerulus.
source: When we looked at each glomerulus, dendrites from different mitral cells were clearly visualized and were distinguishable by their different colors (Figure 5 and Video 3).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 5 and Video 3.

claim: Tetbow can be used to analyze the detailed dendrite wiring diagram of individual M/T cells, including 'sister' M/T cells connected to the same glomerulus.
source: Thus, Tetbow can be used to analyze the detailed dendrite wiring diagram of individual M/T cells, including 'sister' M/T cells, which are connected to the same glomerulus.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of Tetbow.

claim: To clear lipid-rich myelinated axons completely, harsh clearing treatments such as the use of detergents, solvents, and heating are inevitable.
source: However, to clear lipid-rich myelinated axons completely, harsh clearing treatments, such as the use of detergents, solvents, and heating, are inevitable (Dodt et al., 2007; Chung et al., 2013; Renier et al., 2014; Susaki et al., 2014; Murray et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: There is a trade-off between the transparency of tissues and damage to tissues and fluorescent proteins.
source: Indeed, there is a trade-off between the transparency of the tissues and damage to the tissues and fluorescent proteins (Ke et al., 2013; Ke et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Most solvent-based clearing methods, such as BABB, quench fluorescent proteins.
source: For example, most of the solvent-based clearing methods, such as BABB, quench fluorescent proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of solvent-based clearing.

claim: Chemical tags could be a promising alternative to fluorescent proteins to overcome the problem of fluorescent protein quenching.
source: To overcome this problem, chemical tags could be a promising alternative to fluorescent proteins (Kohl et al., 2014; Sutcliffe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Genetically encoded chemical tags such as SNAP, Halo, CLIP, and TMP form covalent bonds with their cognate substrate and fluoresce with synthetic labels.
source: Genetically encoded chemical tags, such as SNAP, Halo, CLIP, and TMP form covalent bonds with their cognate substrate, and fluoresce with synthetic labels.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of chemical tags.

claim: The molecular weights of chemical tag ligands are relatively small, allowing easy penetration into thick tissues.
source: The molecular weights of these ligands are relatively small, allowing easy penetration into thick tissues.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of chemical tags.

claim: Once chemical tags form covalent bonds with their substrates, the fluorescence remains stable even under harsh clearing conditions.
source: Once they form covalent bonds with their substrates, the fluorescence remains stable even under harsh clearing conditions.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of chemical tags.

claim: Three different chemical tags (SNAP, Halo, and CLIP) were tested for Tetbow multicolor labeling.
source: We tested Tetbow multicolor labeling with three different chemical tags, SNAP, Halo, and CLIP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: Chemical tags allowed for robust multicolor labeling of neurons using the Tetbow system.
source: Like fluorescent proteins, chemical tags allowed for the robust multicolor labeling of neurons using the Tetbow system (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 1 mm-thick mouse brain samples were efficiently labeled with chemical tags due to the low molecular weight of the substrates.
source: Owing to the low molecular weight of the substrates, 1 mm-thick mouse brain samples were efficiently labeled (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: After tissue clearing with 3DISCO or BABB, fluorescent proteins were largely quenched.
source: After tissue clearing with solvent-based tissue clearing agents, 3DISCO or BABB, fluorescent proteins were largely quenched (data not shown) (Ke et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated with a citation, though data are not shown in this manuscript.

claim: Synthetic fluorophores bound to chemical tags were bright and stable under 3DISCO or BABB clearing conditions.
source: synthetic fluorophores bound to chemical tags, however, were bright and stable under these clearing conditions (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The size of conventional Brainbow gene cassettes was too large to be packaged into an AAV vector (<5 kb).
source: However, the size of the conventional Brainbow gene cassettes was too large to allow them to be packaged into an AAV vector (<5 kb).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous Brainbow AAV approaches.

claim: A previous study divided the Brainbow cassette into two separate AAVs with two XFP genes each and employed Cre-loxP recombination.
source: For this reason, a previous study divided the Brainbow cassette into two separate AAVs with two XFP genes each, and employed Cre-loxP recombination (Cai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Using the Tetbow strategy with multiple AAV vectors with different XFP genes solves the size problem and achieves improved multicolor labeling using simplified DNA constructs.
source: Using the Tetbow strategy (i.e. multiple AAV vectors with different XFP genes), we can solve the size problem, and achieve improved multicolor labeling using simplified DNA constructs.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the Tetbow AAV approach.

claim: Four separate AAV vectors carrying SYN1-tTA, TRE-mTurquoise2, TRE-EYFP, and TRE-tdTomato genes were generated.
source: We generated four separate AAV vectors carrying SYN1-tTA, TRE-mTurquoise2, TRE-EYFP, and TRE-tdTomato genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the AAV constructs generated.

claim: The human SYNI promoter was used to express tTA specifically in neurons.
source: The human SYNI promoter was used to express tTA specifically in neurons.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the AAV constructs.

claim: Stochastic and combinatorial expression of fluorescent proteins was found in Layer five neurons when AAVs were injected at 4 × 10^8 gc/mL of AAV-SYN1-tTA and 3 × 10^10 gc/mL of AAV-TRE-XFPs.
source: These four AAV vectors (serotype AAV2/1) were injected into the cerebral cortex of adult mice (P56) and analyzed two weeks later. We found a stochastic and combinatorial expression of the encoded fluorescent proteins in Layer five neurons when injected at 4 × 108 gc/mL of AAV-SYN1-tTA and 3 × 1010 gc/mL of AAV-TRE-XFPs (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Virus titer is critical for producing color variations.
source: As expected from our simulation (Figure 1), the virus titer was critical for producing color variations.
evidence: This is stated as a finding consistent with the simulation.

claim: Higher virus titers led to reduced color variations.
source: Higher virus titers led to reduced color variations (Figure 7B, right).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the cerebral cortex, 1-3 × 10^10 gc/mL of AAV-TRE-XFPs was found to be optimum based on expression levels and color variations.
source: In the cerebral cortex, 1–3 × 1010 gc/mL of AAV-TRE-XFPs was found to be optimum on the basis of the resultant expression levels and color variations (Figure 7C and D)
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The optimum virus titer range may be different for different cell types.
source: but the optimum range may be different for different cell types (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), injection volumes, or virus serotypes.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression levels with Tetbow AAVs were sufficiently high for high-resolution imaging of neuronal morphology, including visualization of dendritic spines.
source: Expression levels were sufficiently high for high-resolution imaging of neuronal morphology, including the visualization of dendritic spines (Video 4).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Video 4.

claim: Expression of Tetbow AAVs can lead to toxic effects on cellular functions after prolonged incubation due to extremely high expression levels.
source: It should be noted, however, that the expression of Tetbow AAVs can lead to toxic effects on cellular functions after a prolonged incubation period, as a result of the extremely high levels of expression.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the method.

claim: Cortical neurons started to show aggregation of XFPs and morphological abnormalities 4 weeks after virus injection.
source: For example, cortical neurons started to show an aggregation of XFPs and displayed morphological abnormalities 4 weeks after virus injection, whereas olfactory bulb neurons were best visualized at 4 weeks.
evidence: This is stated as an observation of toxicity.

claim: The optimum incubation time may be different for different cell types.
source: Thus, the optimum incubation time may be different for different cell types.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: Tetbow is particularly useful for analysis of long-range axonal projection of a population of neurons.
source: The bright multicolor labeling method, Tetbow, is particularly useful for the analysis of long-range axonal projection of a population of neurons.
evidence: This is stated as an application of the method.

claim: Mitral and tufted (M/T) cells in the olfactory bulb project axons up to several millimeters to the olfactory cortex.
source: To test the utility of Tetbow, we focused on mitral and tufted (M/T) cells in the olfactory bulb, which project axons (up to several millimeters) to the olfactory cortex, including the anterior olfactory nucleus, olfactory tubercle, piriform cortex, cortical amygdala, and lateral entorhinal cortex.
evidence: This describes the biological system studied.

claim: Previous studies performed axon tracing on populations of M/T cells from glomeruli using dye injections but could not fully dissect individual axons.
source: Previous studies have performed axon tracing on populations of M/T cells from glomeruli in the olfactory bulb using dye injections (Nagayama, 2010; Sosulski et al., 2011), but these studies could not fully dissect individual axons.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Other studies performed single-cell axon tracing using hundreds of serial brain sections, but these analyses were highly laborious and time-consuming.
source: Other studies performed single-cell axon tracing using hundreds of serial brain sections, but these analyses were highly laborious and time-consuming (Ghosh et al., 2011; Igarashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: We do not yet fully understand how odor inputs into individual M/T cells are conveyed to the olfactory cortex.
source: Owing to these limitations, we do not yet understand fully how the odor inputs into individual M/T cells are conveyed to the olfactory cortex.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Compared to single-color labeling, the stochastic and combinatorial expression of XFPs was helpful in improving tracing performance.
source: When compared to single-color labeling, the stochastic and combinatorial expression of XFPs was helpful in improving tracing performance (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Efficient axon tracing was facilitated by local injection of Tetbow AAVs.
source: Efficient axon tracing was further facilitated by the local injection of Tetbow AAVs (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: In the olfactory bulb, many types of neurons were labeled, but only M/T cells projected their axons to the olfactory cortex.
source: In the olfactory bulb, many types of neurons were labeled, but only M/T cells projected their axons to the olfactory cortex.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: The olfactory cortical area was flattened onto a glass slide to facilitate high-resolution fluorescence imaging with limited working distance of the objective lens.
source: To facilitate high-resolution fluorescence imaging with a limited working distance of the objective lens (20x, NA = 0.75, WD = 0.66 mm), we flattened the olfactory cortical area onto a glass slide (Sosulski et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach with citation.

claim: After fixation and tissue clearing, axons of individual M/T cells were clearly visualized with XFPs in the entire area of the olfactory cortex.
source: After the fixation and tissue clearing, axons of individual M/T cells were clearly visualized with XFPs in the entire area of the olfactory cortex (Figure 8D and Video 5).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 8D and Video 5.

claim: The unique color hue was largely preserved at the average level from proximal to distal part in each axon.
source: The unique color hue was largely preserved at the average level, if not at a single-pixel resolution, from proximal to distal part in each axon (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Across three image areas, the median Euclidean distance for the same neuron was 0.049 (interquartile range = 0.063, n = 34 pairs).
source: Across the three image areas, the median Euclidean distance for the same neuron was 0.049 (interquartile range = 0.063, n = 34 pairs).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative measure of color consistency.

claim: The unique color hues and their consistency facilitated manual reconstruction of individual M/T cell axons in the olfactory cortex.
source: The unique color hues and their consistency facilitated manual reconstruction of individual M/T cell axons in the olfactory cortex (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 2, and Video 6).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 2, and Video 6.

claim: Highly divergent patterns of axonal collaterals were observed among labeled M/T cell axons.
source: Highly divergent patterns of axonal collaterals were observed among labeled M/T cell axons, complementing earlier findings (Nagayama, 2010; Ghosh et al., 2011; Sosulski et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The Cre-loxP system is not essential for stochastic and combinatorial expression of XFP genes in vector-mediated gene transfer.
source: However, in the vector-mediated gene transfer, the Cre-loxP system is not essential for the stochastic and combinatorial expression of XFP genes (Kobiler et al., 2010; Weber et al., 2011; Siddiqi et al., 2014).
evidence: This implies that simpler approaches can achieve the same goal.

claim: Tetbow overcomes the trade-off between expression levels and color variations that limited previous Brainbow methods.
source: Thus, there is a trade-off between the expression levels of fluorescent proteins and color variations, and this is the reason why the previous Brainbow methods were unable to produce color variations that were bright enough for labeling.
evidence: This is implied by the discussion of the trade-off and the development of Tetbow to address it.

claim: The maximum length of traced axon was 6852.63 μm.
source: The maximum length of the traced axon was 6852.63 μm.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative result.

claim: Axon tracing was terminated when labeled axons were interrupted by unlabeled gaps, making the tracing conservative and likely an underestimate of the entire wiring diagram.
source: We terminated tracing when the labeled axons were interrupted by unlabeled gaps. Thus, our conservative tracing is most probably showing an underestimate of the entire wiring diagram.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological limitation.

claim: Color hues were consistent at a global scale but not perfect in high-magnification images.
source: Color hues were consistent at a global scale (Figure 8E), but not perfect in high-magnification images (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to figures.

claim: Chromatic aberration can be a problem in high-resolution imaging of thick tissues.
source: Chromatic aberration can also be a problem in the high-resolution imaging of thick tissues.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation.

claim: An important challenge is to improve color hue consistency throughout a neuron and develop auto-tracing software optimized for multicolor-labeled neurons.
source: Another important challenge will be to improve the color hue consistency throughout a neuron and to develop auto-tracing software that is optimized for the multicolor-labeled neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a future direction.
